questions.question: What is Bayes' rule for events $A$ and $B$ with positive probabilities?
options: $P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}$
$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}$
$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(B)}{P(A)}$
$P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)$

questions.question: What is Bayes' rule mainly used for?
options: Computing the probability that two events occur together
Splitting a probability into cases of a partition
Updating a belief after new evidence is observed
Checking whether two events are independent

questions.question: Which two conditional probabilities are connected by Bayes' rule?
options: $P(A)$ and $P(A^c)$ only
$P(A\cup B)$ and $P(A\cap B)$ only
$P(S)$ and $P(\varnothing)$ only
$P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B\mid A)$

questions.question: What probabilities are required in the simple two-event Bayes formula?
options: $P(B\mid A)$, $P(A)$, and $P(B)$
Only $P(A\cup B)$
Only $P(A^c)$
Only the total number of equally likely outcomes, with no event counts

questions.question: How is Bayes' rule obtained?
options: By assuming that $A$ and $B$ are independent events
By setting $\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)$ equal to $\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)$ directly
By writing $\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)$ two ways via conditioning
By writing $\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)$ in two ways by inclusion-exclusion

questions.question: If $P(B\mid A)=0.8$, $P(A)=0.1$, and $P(B)=0.2$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
Which example naturally uses Bayes' rule?
options: Updating spam probability after observing words.
Arranging five books on a shelf
Counting identical candies among boxes
Finding the complement of a single die event only.

questions.question: In a diagnostic-test setting, which probability is a posterior probability?
options: The probability of a positive test given disease
The unconditional prevalence alone
The number of possible test outcomes
The probability of disease given a positive test

questions.question: If $P(B\mid A)=0.6$, $P(A)=0.5$, and $P(B)=0.3$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
In reliability analysis, what can be inferred using Bayes' rule after an observed failure pattern?
options: A component type, using prior frequencies.
The number of unordered card hands
The exact calendar birthday of each one of the components.
The empty event probability only

questions.question: Why do base rates matter in Bayes' rule?
options: They enter via the likelihoods, not via the priors
They enter via priors and affect posteriors
They matter only when the evidence is weak or noisy
They cancel between the numerator and the denominator

questions.question: What is the denominator in the partition form of Bayes' rule?
options: $\sum_j P(B\mid A_j)P(A_j)$
$\sum_j P(A_j\mid B)P(A_j)$
$P(B\mid A_i)P(A_i)$
$\sum_j P(B\mid A_j)$

questions.question: Why is Bayes' rule helpful when $P(B\mid A)$ is easier than $P(A\mid B)$?
options: It shows the two conditionals are equal, so either may be used
It converts the easier conditional into the reverse direction
It gives $P(A\mid B)$ from $P(B\mid A)$ alone, without any prior
It applies only when $A$ and $B$ are independent events

questions.question: A disease has prevalence $0.01$, sensitivity $0.90$, and positive-test probability $0.05$. What is $P(\text{disease}\mid\text{positive})$?
Suppose $A_1,A_2$ partition the space, with $P(A_1)=0.3$, $P(A_2)=0.7$, $P(B\mid A_1)=0.4$, and $P(B\mid A_2)=0.1$. What is the denominator for $P(A_1\mid B)$?
If $P(B\mid A)=0.2$, $P(A)=0.4$, and $P(B)=0.5$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
What mistake does Bayes' rule help avoid?
options: Subtracting the empty set from the sample space
Confusing $P(B\mid A)$ with $P(A\mid B)$
Counting combinations as unordered groups
Using a partition with nonempty sets

questions.question: Why can a highly sensitive test still have low positive predictive value?
options: Most sick people test negative, so true positives are few
A rare disease lets false positives dominate positives
A common disease lets false positives outnumber true ones
The predictive value equals one minus the sensitivity

questions.question: Using the partition form, if $P(A_1)=0.2$, $P(A_2)=0.8$, $P(B\mid A_1)=0.9$, and $P(B\mid A_2)=0.1$, what is $P(A_1\mid B)$?
A rare component type has prior probability $0.02$ and produces a failure pattern with probability $0.8$. The overall failure-pattern probability is $0.10$. What posterior expression follows?
